claims.text: In-situ powder-bed preheating during LPBF reduces thermal gradients in high-entropy-alloy components.
Reduced thermal gradients from preheating lower residual stresses.
Powder-bed preheating improves the dimensional precision of LPBF high-entropy-alloy components.
Powder-bed preheating improves mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects.
HEA components made by standard LPBF without preheating typically exhibit significant porosity.
HEA components made by standard LPBF without preheating typically exhibit thermal-stress-induced distortion.
A controlled powder-bed temperature of 400–600 °C is an appropriate moderate preheating range for the proposed intervention.
The intervention should apply to refractory or eutectic high-entropy alloys processed by LPBF.
Using an argon environment and low-oxygen powder during preheating minimizes oxidation risk.
Preheating stabilizes microstructural evolution and may promote beneficial short-range order.
Lower thermal gradients and residual stresses limit porosity and microcracking associated with rapid solidification.
Preheating diminishes thermal shock and abrupt cooling, producing slower and more uniform solidification.
Slower, more uniform solidification moderates contraction stresses and decreases nucleation of porosity and cracks.
Preheating-induced short-range ordering can stabilize dislocation motion and enhance mechanical integrity.
Relative to conventional LPBF, preheated components should have lower porosity and residual stress.
Relative to conventional LPBF, preheated components should exhibit less warpage and deviation from intended dimensions.
Preheating may increase yield or compressive strength by 10–20%.
The intervention is limited to alloys that tolerate elevated temperatures without oxidation or unwanted phase transformations.
Excessive preheating can cause powder coalescence or deleterious microstructural changes.
